seo.title: Karmic tail 6 14 8 compatibility: Pride and Prejudice in a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 14 8 compatibility: The Lovers at the entry, Temperance in the middle, Justice as the main task and The Tower at the centre in 9 couples of 10.

title: Karmic tail 6-14-8 in compatibility: from first impressions to a fair verdict
short: In nine couples out of ten with the karmic tail 6-14-8, the centre of the matrix holds The Tower, the card of sudden collapse. It is an odd neighbour for a tail that opens with The Lovers and closes with Justice. The answer to the riddle is that 6-14-8 is not a story about love at first sight but about putting first sight on trial. The couple enters the task through attraction and a first opinion of each other, lives it as a slow blending of two characters, and learns the main thing: to judge fairly — each other, themselves and what happened between them. The Tower at the centre is the moment when an opinion built on a first impression falls down. More than two hundred years ago Jane Austen wrote this plot.

sections.h2: The novel that was first called First Impressions
paragraphs: In October 1796 the twenty-year-old Jane Austen sat down to a novel and finished it by the following August. It was called First Impressions. Her father offered the manuscript to the London publisher Thomas Cadell and was turned down. Sixteen years later, in January 1813, the reworked book came out under another title: Pride and Prejudice.

Austen took the new title from someone else's novel. In Fanny Burney's Cecilia (1782), Dr Lyster sums up the heroes' troubles, and two words of his speech are printed in capitals: "The whole of this unfortunate business has been the result of PRIDE and PREJUDICE." Then comes the sentence worth remembering him for: "if to PRIDE and PREJUDICE you owe your miseries, so wonderfully is good and evil balanced, that to PRIDE and PREJUDICE you will also owe their termination."

The two titles of one book are the two ends of the tail 6-14-8. First Impressions is the entry, The Lovers: attraction, choice, an instant judgement. "So wonderfully is good and evil balanced" is the scales of Justice, the main task. Between them lie a long middle and an explosion at the centre. Many remember the plot: at a ball the proud Mr Darcy makes a cutting remark about Elizabeth Bennet, she believes the handsome story told by the charming Wickham, Darcy unexpectedly proposes and is refused with accusations, he answers with a letter — and from then on the two slowly revise their view of each other. Austen named the novel not after love but after what stands in love's way.

sections.h2: The Lovers at the entry: a first impression is already a verdict
paragraphs: Point M in a couple's tail is the "Entry to the task": what the two want together, what they agree on, what language they speak. The couple enters the task through this wish. But the point stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish easily becomes resistance.

The novel opens with a law nobody ever passed: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife." The neighbours have not yet seen the new tenant of Netherfield, and he already "is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters." A few pages later comes the first ball, and the verdict is passed in a single evening. For the first half of the evening Darcy is admired; then "his character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world." He returns the favour: Elizabeth, in his words, is "tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me."

Waite's divinatory list for The Lovers opens with the words "Attraction, love, beauty." At the entry of this couple, attraction arrives together with an assessment: handsome or not, one of us or a stranger, suitable or "not handsome enough." Benebell Wen writes of The Lovers in love readings that "there is a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning," but "not all is as it seems." In the novel the paradise of first sight goes to Wickham: "His countenance, voice, and manner, had established him at once in the possession of every virtue." Neither of Elizabeth's two first impressions will prove right.

In a 6-14-8 couple this looks quite ordinary. The story of how they met, told to guests, is already a small verdict: "he didn't even look my way that night," "I thought she was terribly stuck-up." Nicknames and jokes grow out of those first judgements, and a common language grows out of the jokes. While the language is funny, it binds. When a role gets stuck in it — "you're always like that" — each starts proving that the first opinion was a mistake, or, on the contrary, that it was right. In Yuliana Lisovskaya's account, The Lovers at their worst mean idealisation, perfectionism and the insecurity from which jealousy and control grow. At this entry they are easy to recognise: one keeps checking whether they are still looked at as on the first evening, the other feels constantly assessed.

sections.h2: The Tower at the centre: a house built on a first opinion
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the "Atmosphere": what happens between two people when nobody is watching. In 89.6% of couples with the tail 6-14-8 it holds The Tower; in the remaining 10.4%, The Chariot. There is no third option.

The scene at Hunsford, one of the best known in the novel, is The Tower itself. Darcy declares his love in such a way that the declaration sounds like a list of arguments against it: inequality, damage to his name, the bride's relations. Elizabeth answers just as directly, and her central sentence is built like an account of a construction site: his manners, from the first moment of their acquaintance, "were such as to form that groundwork of disapprobation, on which succeeding events have built so immovable a dislike." Darcy sums it up like a bookkeeper: "My faults, according to this calculation, are heavy indeed!" Within one day both buildings will fall: his certainty that he cannot be refused, and her certainty about Wickham.

Now take Benebell Wen's description of The Tower (Holistic Tarot, 2015). Upright, the card is a downfall through pride and ego: "the Seeker's ego will be struck down to humility. This is good news, actually. There will be a lesson in humility." Reversed, it is the jolt felt by someone who "relied on false impressions made by others"; sometimes, someone who "has been falsely accused." And after the jolt, in Wen's words, "the aftermath is truth." Pride, false impressions taken from someone else's words, a false accusation and truth after the blow — this is not the theme of the novel but its main events, and in the same order.

A calculated card has no upright or reversed position: the number 16 at the centre lies neither way. The couple gets the whole Tower, both halves of the description. In the novel they went to two people: the pride to Darcy, the borrowed impressions to Elizabeth. In a living couple the halves are not handed out as roles: pride and trust in other people's stories are found in each partner. And the "lesson in humility" returns word for word at the end of the book, in Darcy's mouth: "You taught me a lesson, hard indeed at first, but most advantageous. By you, I was properly humbled."

Among the tasks of a couple with The Tower, Lisovskaya names the collapse of an invented image of the partner, and in her reading of a couple with The Tower at the centre she warns that what is said in a quarrel stays in the memory. Austen shows it literally: months later Darcy repeats her reproof word for word — "Had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner" — and admits how those words have tortured him. The Tower at the centre does not predict disasters. It describes how truth comes to this couple: not drop by drop, but in a blow, when the accumulated opinion can no longer bear its own weight. A quarrel in such a couple is rarely about an unwashed mug. It is about "you've been like this from the very start…" — and at that moment one can see how many storeys have been added on top of the first impression.

One more clue lies in the arithmetic. In a personal matrix, the entry to the tail equals the sum of the task and the centre. A couple's matrix is not calculated that way, yet in 6-14-8 with The Tower the formula holds by itself: Justice plus The Tower, 8 + 16 = 24 → 2 + 4 = 6, gives The Lovers. Scales plus collapse — love again. In the novel the second proposal comes only after the collapse and after an honest reckoning. With The Chariot at the centre the equation does not work: 8 + 7 = 15.

sections.h2: Darcy's letter: a speech for the defence on two charges
paragraphs: The couple's main task, point D, is Justice. Lisovskaya reads this point mostly through its minus: what the couple does not manage and what it has to learn. Austen shows both the minus and the way out of it in a single chapter.

The morning after the refusal Darcy hands Elizabeth a letter: two sheets "written quite through, in a very close hand," and even the envelope full. It is a real speech for the defence. "Two offences of a very different nature, and by no means of equal magnitude, you last night laid to my charge," he begins, answers each in turn, offers a witness and asks not for pity but for a hearing: "I demand it of your justice." Elizabeth reads like a judge trying not to decide in advance: she "weighed every circumstance with what she meant to be impartiality — deliberated on the probability of each statement — but with little success. On both sides it was only assertion." The scales stand level. What tips them is not a new argument but a second reading.

And then the main thing happens: Elizabeth passes her first fair verdict not on Darcy, not on Wickham, but on herself. "How humiliating is this discovery! Yet, how just a humiliation! … But vanity, not love, has been my folly. Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted prepossession and ignorance… Till this moment, I never knew myself." The last sentence is the shortest of all, and the heaviest.

Waite's list for Justice reversed ends with the words "bigotry, bias, excessive severity"; bias is prejudice by another name. Wen sums the card up in one formula: upright, "What is fair will feel fair"; reversed, "what is fair will not feel fair." That is an exact description of the minute over the letter: everything Darcy writes is true, and that is precisely why it is unbearable to read.

In a 6-14-8 couple, Justice at its worst rarely looks like a court with a sword. More often it is a quiet habit of measuring the partner by oneself and not noticing what hurts them; of displaying their faults to look better; of collecting evidence instead of asking. One partner ends up as prosecutor, the other as defendant; the roles may swap, but the court never rises. The tasks Lisovskaya sets a couple with Justice repeat Elizabeth's road: to admit one's own fault instead of blaming everyone; to forgive; to let go of idealising the partner. Justice does not prove that anyone deserved their grievance. It asks which scales the grievance was weighed on.

sections.h2: Temperance in the middle: on Waite's card the water flows uphill
paragraphs: The middle of the tail, point N, has no meaning of its own for Lisovskaya — it is an "addition" to the main task. We read it as the road: what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish at the entry to the task at the end. In 6-14-8 that road is Temperance.

Austen, unusually, names it outright. When Elizabeth, after the letter and after the visit to Pemberley, realises that her feelings have changed, the author steps into the story herself: "If gratitude and esteem are good foundations of affection, Elizabeth's change of sentiment will be neither improbable nor faulty." And she compares it with the other way of falling in love — with what "is so often described as arising on a first interview with its object, and even before two words have been exchanged." Elizabeth has already tried the first way on Wickham and now turns to "the other less interesting mode of attachment." Austen's word is pointedly dry. Two ways of loving in one paragraph — exactly the entry and the middle of the tail: The Lovers at first sight and Temperance, which blends feeling slowly, out of esteem and gratitude.

For Wen, Temperance "is the fusion of two contrasting elements and bringing them into harmony," and for a couple it suggests "a greater need for cooperation and tempering of extreme emotions, such as anger, resentment, hostility." On Waite's card an angel pours water between two cups, and Wen asks an unexpected question: does the water flow "from the higher cup to the lower cup, with gravity, or from the lower cup to the higher cup, against gravity, against the laws of physics"? In Austen the water flows uphill. Darcy is richer, better born and eight years older, yet it is Elizabeth who teaches him. He admits it himself: "As a child I was taught what was right, but I was not taught to correct my temper." Temper and temperance are one word at the root.

There is a clue in the numbers too. Card 14 does not appear in the personal tail of either partner — not in any of the nine combinations that add up to 6-14-8. The couple's middle is something nobody brought along. It is gathered from the two personal middles: in 42% of such couples it is The Hermit and The Hierophant (9 + 5), in 30% The Lovers and Justice (6 + 8), in 16% The Wheel of Fortune and The Emperor (10 + 4), in 12% two Chariots (7 + 7). In almost a third of couples, one partner carries The Lovers in the middle of their personal tail and the other carries Justice, and only together do they make Temperance. Even without that coincidence, the middle of 6-14-8 equals the sum of its ends exactly: 6 + 8 = 14. A couple's middle is never worked out from the outer numbers, but here it adds up — Temperance literally blends The Lovers and Justice.

In a living couple the middle is work that cannot be seen from outside. Two people blend two ways of life: in one family they quarrelled loudly and made up at once, in the other they went silent for a week. One apologises in words, the other in deeds, and neither notices the other's apologies. Lisovskaya advises a couple with Temperance to catch how the partner speaks of love, since everyone does it in their own way. Darcy declares himself in deeds: he secretly finds the runaway Lydia and settles her fate, and when Elizabeth thanks him on her family's behalf he replies: "your family owe me nothing. Much as I respect them, I believe I thought only of you." At its worst, Temperance means one partner always gives way and the other does not notice: the water pours in one direction only. And Lisovskaya's advice not to jump to conclusions about the partner reads like a direct antidote to "first impressions."

sections.h2: Justice as the main task: blame shared in half
paragraphs: When the two finally have it out, Austen stages a strange argument. Darcy asks: "What did you say of me that I did not deserve? … my behaviour to you at the time had merited the severest reproof." Elizabeth will not let him take it all: "We will not quarrel for the greater share of blame annexed to that evening. The conduct of neither, if strictly examined, will be irreproachable." The two argue about who is more to blame, and each pulls the larger share towards himself or herself.

This is a couple's Justice at its best: not a verdict on one of the two, but blame shared in half. The first thing Darcy does after the reconciliation is to go to his friend and confess that his "former interference in his affairs" was "absurd and impertinent"; the friend forgives him. A Justice that began with accusations ends with a confession.

Austen adds to the scales the one thing without which they turn into bookkeeping. Darcy hopes the letter has been destroyed, and Elizabeth promises: "The letter shall certainly be burnt." She sets out her philosophy: "Think only of the past as its remembrance gives you pleasure." Darcy objects: "Painful recollections will intrude, which cannot, which ought not to be repelled." Both are right. Justice in a 6-14-8 couple means keeping the lesson and burning the case file: not bringing a closed case back into every new quarrel.

It has a third face as well — equality. Lady Catherine de Bourgh arrives to forbid the engagement and exclaims: "Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?" Elizabeth answers with a formula worthy of the scales: "He is a gentleman; I am a gentleman's daughter; so far we are equal." Not equality of fortune — equality of standing. Burney promised that pride and prejudice would themselves end the miseries, and Austen keeps her word: Lady Catherine's pride brings Darcy back. Her account of the conversation with Elizabeth, he says, "taught me to hope."

Justice at its best, for Lisovskaya, means a fair division of duties, restraint in words, "a cool head and a warm heart." In a couple with this tail it shows in small things: a hurt is named aloud the same day, not a year later on a general list; the argument is about the deed, not the character; "I was wrong" is heard no less often than "you were wrong."

sections.h2: The couple's values: The World, The Hanged Man and The Empress
paragraphs: "The couple's values" is the spiritual purpose, one more answer to the question of why the two met. In couples with the tail 6-14-8 only three cards appear here: The World in 51.1%, The Hanged Man in 26.8%, The Empress in 22.1%. What follows is our reading, not a statement from the books.

Wen describes The World as "the supreme balance between good and evil, a complete reconciliation of the universe's dichotomy and duality" — almost Dr Lyster's words about good and evil "so wonderfully balanced." For half of these couples the value is a whole in which both pride and prejudice have found their place, and there is no longer any need to settle whose share was bigger. Waite's list for The Hanged Man begins with "Wisdom, circumspection, discernment," and Elizabeth reproached herself precisely over her discernment: "I, who have prided myself on my discernment!" The value of The Hanged Man is clear sight that comes once one's view has been turned upside down. Waite's Empress is above all "Fruitfulness"; Austen's ending is the house at Pemberley, where the closest friends are Elizabeth's uncle and aunt Gardiner — the very relations whose condition in life Darcy once called "so decidedly beneath my own," and who, "by bringing her into Derbyshire, had been the means of uniting them."

Each point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. A person born on 11.02.1976 has the personal tail 9-9-18; a person born on 14.08.1975 has 15-5-8.

The middle comes from the two personal middles, 9 and 5, and is not worked out from the entry and the task. The centre of this couple is 9 + 7 = 16, The Tower, as in most such couples. "Image of the couple" is The Chariot (11 + 14 = 25 → 7), "What to create together" is The Wheel of Fortune (2 + 8 = 10), "Values" is The Empress.

Justice appears twice in this couple: in the main task and at the point "What fills" (13 + 22 = 35 → 8). A repeat does not double the card — each point has its own role. In the task, Justice is read through what does not work yet; in "What fills", through what gives the couple back its strength. The same honest conversation that comes hardest is also what restores the union after a hard stretch.

The combination of the personal tails 15-5-8 and 9-9-18 is the most common route to 6-14-8: 23% of such couples are built this way. The second partner already has Justice at the end of the personal tail, but that says nothing about who is the "judge" in the couple: a personal tail and a couple's tail are calculated differently, and their points mean different things.

sections.h2: Which personal tails add up to 6-14-8
paragraphs: The tail 6-14-8 occurs in roughly one couple in 62 (1.621%) and ranks 21st of the 97 couple tails. It comes from nine combinations of personal tails; the most common are 15-5-8 + 9-9-18 (23% of such couples), 18-6-6 + 6-8-20 (20%) and 18-9-9 + 6-5-17 (19%).
In 28% of couples neither partner has The Lovers, Temperance or Justice in their personal tail. A couple's tail is not the sum of two characters but a new plot that appears only when there are two.

No other couple tails are made of these three numbers: the entry to a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and the order 6-8-14 does not occur in any couple. The order 6-14-8 also exists as a personal karmic tail — for 55 dates since 1900 — but that is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article about it.
The tail passes no sentence on the union. It shows where this couple's knot is and what unties it.

ul: **Check the first opinion.** What is it built on — one's own experience or someone else's story, as with Elizabeth and Wickham?
**Argue about the deed, not the character.** The phrase "you've been like this from the very start…" adds another storey to The Tower.
**Share the blame out loud.** When both are at fault, don't compete over who is more to blame — in accusation or in repentance.
**Reread the letter.** Elizabeth understood Darcy on the second reading; an important conversation deserves a second attempt.
**Take turns giving way.** Notice who in the couple always gives way, and swap roles.
**Burn the case file.** Don't bring a closed case into a new quarrel.

paragraphs: If quarrels turn into threats, stalking or fear for one's safety, this is no longer a task of the tail but a reason to call a local emergency number and seek a psychologist's help.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — The Lovers (6).** What the couple wants together: attraction, choosing each other, a common language. This is also where the first opinion of each other is born, and the same wish can turn into resistance.

**N · Middle of the task — Temperance (14).** How the couple walks the road: blending two characters and looking for the measure at which both can live. Neither partner brings this card into the couple.

**D · Main task — Justice (8).** What there is to learn: to judge without bias and without keeping score of grievances, to own one's share of the blame, to see the other as an equal. It is read mostly through what does not work yet.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-14-8 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the couple's tasks in the order M–N–D. The entry is The Lovers: attraction, choice, a common language and a first opinion of each other. The middle is Temperance: a slow blending of two characters. The main task is Justice: a fair verdict on oneself and the partner, blame shared in half, equality. The key point is Justice; the other two unfold it.

faq.q: Is the tail 6-14-8 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events and does not decide whether two people suit each other. It shows where the couple stumbles and what it learns: to revise first impressions and to judge fairly. This method gives no compatibility percentages.

faq.q: Why do such couples almost always have The Tower at the centre?
faq.a: The numbers of the tail and the centre are linked: in every personal matrix the entry to the tail equals the task plus the centre, and this kinship survives when two matrices are added. So a couple with the tail 6-14-8 can only have 16 or 7 at the centre, and The Tower comes up in 89.6% of couples. It describes the atmosphere: truth arrives in a blow, when an opinion built on a first impression collapses.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 6-14-8 differ from the personal tail 6-14-8?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date and occurs for 55 dates since 1900; its points mean something else. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two matrices, reduced to 22, and it is read as the tasks of the union. Readings cannot be carried over from one to the other.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. The entry to a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 8 and 14 never stand at the entry, and the order 6-8-14 does not occur in any couple. Of the numbers 6, 14 and 8, only the couple tail 6-14-8 can be formed.
